summary: For 7–8 year olds learning how shadows form: a shadow is the region where an opaque object blocks light from reaching a surface (the absence of light), NOT a reflection or dark copy of the object. The key teaching move is cognitive conflict — resize the shadow by moving the object toward or away from the light while the object itself stays the same size, something a reflection or copy could not do. Learners also run a measured fair test of the distance–size pattern (for a torch close by, closer to the light source = bigger shadow) and observe that the shadow always falls on the side away from the light. Observe the shadow where it falls on the wall rather than looking at the light itself. The full straight-line ray account of why the shadow matches the outline is formalised later.
misconceptions: A shadow is a reflection or a dark image/copy of the object (so its shape must always match exactly, like a 'dark reflection').
A shadow is a thing or object in its own right — it exists in the dark, just unseen, and is revealed by light.
A shadow belongs to / comes from within the object and simply follows it around.
Shadow size depends only on the size of the object, not on the object's distance from the light.
Shadows only occur outdoors or only in the daytime.
The object 'absorbs' the light and that is the shadow, rather than the shadow being the unlit region beyond the object.

activities.title: Resize the shadow: a shadow is blocked light, not a copy
steps: Set up a light source, an opaque shape (e.g. a star or toy), and a wall or screen in a darkened space so a clear shadow is cast on the wall.

Slide the object toward the light and watch the shadow on the wall grow larger; slide it back toward the wall and watch the shadow shrink — noting the whole time that the object itself has NOT changed size.

State out loud: the object stayed the same size, but the shadow grew and shrank as the object moved between the light and the wall, so the shadow is not a fixed dark copy of the object — it is the part of the wall the object is keeping the light off.

Keeping the object and wall in place, move the light from one side of the object (e.g. left) across to the other side (right) and watch the shadow on the wall move the opposite way (the shadow always falls on the side of the object away from the light).
Swap the opaque shape for a translucent one and observe the shadow go pale, linking back to transparent/translucent/opaque materials.
activities.insight: A shadow is the absence of light where an opaque object blocks light from reaching a surface; it is not a reflection, dark copy, or an object the thing carries around. Its size changes as the object moves between the light and the wall while the object itself stays the same size, which fits blocked light rather than a fixed copy of the object.

activities.title: Measured fair test: the distance–size pattern
steps: In a darkened room, use a torch, an opaque object, and a blank wall, with a ruler or tape measure to measure the shadow on the wall.
Decide which single thing to vary — the object's distance from the torch — and keep the torch and wall fixed so it is a fair test.
Before each trial, predict whether the shadow will be bigger or smaller, then measure the shadow and record object-distance against shadow-size in a results table.
Complete a pattern sentence stem from the results, e.g. 'the closer the object is to the light source, the bigger the shadow'.
Explain why: with the small nearby torch, closer to the source the object blocks a wider spread of the straight-travelling light, so the shadow grows.
activities.insight: Shadow size depends on the object's distance from the light source, not only on the size of the object; with a small nearby source (a torch), moving the object toward the light makes the shadow larger because it blocks a wider cone of spreading light.

activities.title: Predict-explain-test: outline or copy?
steps: Look at a toy standing in front of a lamp casting a shadow on the wall. Predict whether the shadow will show the toy's FRONT — its face and colours — or only its outline shape, and say why BEFORE testing.
Also predict whether the shadow gets bigger or smaller when the toy slides toward the lamp, and say why.
Test both predictions and explain what you see.
Consider the counterexample: if the toy were made of clear glass instead, would it cast the same dark shadow? Explain your reasoning.
Consider: could there be a shadow with no light at all in the room? What does a shadow actually need to exist?
activities.insight: The shadow can only be a featureless dark outline, because it is the region where the opaque object blocked light from reaching the wall — it cannot be a picture (face/colours) of the object. A clear/transparent object lets light through, so it does not cast a dark shadow like an opaque one; without a light source there is no shadow at all.

activities.title: Diagnose prior ideas and check understanding
steps: At the start, surface prior ideas with a diagnostic prompt (e.g. BEST 'A penguin's shadow' / 'Making a shadow'): does a shadow show the object's front and colours, or just its outline, and why?
Answer a short check: is a shadow a reflection of the object? (expect resistance and probe the reasoning, not just the answer).
Given a lamp and object at stated positions, predict the relative size of the shadow and explain the reasoning.
Describe what happens to the shadow as the object moves from near the wall to near the lamp, and why.
activities.insight: Learners can state that a shadow is blocked light (not a reflection) and can predict and justify the distance–size pattern — and recognise that conceptual change may need several experiences, not a single telling.

checkQuestion: A toy stands in front of a lamp and casts a shadow on the wall. Does the shadow show the toy's FRONT — its face and its colours — or only its outline shape? Explain why the shadow looks the way it does.
checkAnswer: Only the outline shape — a dark silhouette, with no face and no colours. The shadow is the region where the opaque toy has blocked light from reaching the wall, so it can only be the shape of the block, not a picture of the toy.
